source.title: Grounding Functional Similarity by Invariance-Aware Model Stitching
source.authors: Ioannis Athanasiadis; Anmar Karmush; Michael Felsberg

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Some results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text.
record.tranche_reason: The study compares stitching-based functional similarity under different alignment objectives and input manipulations, and reports that standard stitching can obscure functional discrepancies. It refines when representation interchangeability is a meaningful similarity measure.
record.gate_note: The paper reports qualitative outcomes for stitching curves and comparisons between standard and invariance-aware stitching. Numerical curve values are not stated in the text. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study argues, with results, that standard affine stitching overstates functional interchangeability. Models using different cues, or stitching layers exploiting unseen shortcuts, still look compatible. An invariance-aware variant changes the verdicts. This bears on V4 (stitching-based interchangeability) and V6 (convergence depends on the measure and inputs). It does not test scale, cross-modal alignment, universal features or causes of convergence.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct as paraphrased. The authors conclude that standard stitching probes only forward compatibility and can overstate similarity or exploit unseen cues. Invariance-aware stitching exposes hidden discrepancies, including between robust and non-robust models. No objective is optimal across architectures; there is a trade-off between high similarity and avoiding unseen cues.
record.recipe_differences: Uses affine model stitching to evaluate functional compatibility, with a new invariance-aware procedure based on identically represented inputs and an additional FuLA objective. It is not a scale or distance-geometry convergence experiment of the original claim sources.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with stitching objective (HLM, SLM, DM, FuLA), standard versus invariance-aware data, shortcut availability, model architecture, robust versus non-robust training, and clean versus adversarial samples. In the additional architecture experiments, shortcut mitigation and relative similarity also vary by architecture and objective.

fits_no_version.finding: Under invariance-aware stitching, adversarially robust models are functionally more similar to each other than any other configuration, across ResNet-18, VGG-16 and ViT-Tiny.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Adversarial robustness increases functional convergence between independently trained models.

record.problems: The study is limited to image-classification models. The authors state that there is no oracle notion of functional similarity, so they cannot determine definitively which setting most faithfully reflects similarity. Many results are qualitative figure trajectories without numerical values in the text. Experiments report averages across three random initializations, but no error bars or other uncertainty estimates are stated. The authors also note that relaxed identically represented inputs and data augmentation can affect the operationalization; their augmentation control had minimal effect.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results omitted under the 60-row limit. Qualitative detailed trajectories in Appendices F.2–F.4 and G are represented in aggregate where the text states an aggregate trend; individual figure-only curve values are not separately transcribed.

untested.parts: No sweep over model size or capability.
No vision-language or paired cross-modal comparison.
Cross-seed ResNet-18 pairs are stitched, but only figure curves are reported. There is no analysis of shared features or subspaces versus individual units or bases.
No interpretable features, neurons, SAE features or circuits measured.
No test of whether shared data or objectives explain alignment, nor of plateaus with scale.

missing.what: Separate identity, cross-seed and cross-supervised trajectories (with the progressively sharper drop) under invariance-aware stitching; currently pooled in r2
SLM fails the identity-stitching sanity check for ViT-Base on ImageNet-100; DM is an exception to high cross-bias similarity under standard stitching
Optimal objective differs by architecture: DM best at removing cue exploitation for ViT-Tiny, SLM highest similarity in transformers at the cost of more cue use

record.verdict_notes: All results are qualitative figure trajectories averaged over 3 runs, with no numbers or error bars in the text. Image classification only. The V7 links were removed from all rows because nothing addresses causes of convergence. This study is not among the original sources.

versions.untested_parts: No scaling sweep or comparison of model size and capability.
No vision-language or other cross-modal paired-data comparison.
The paper includes cross-seed stitching, but does not measure shared features or subspaces, or whether individual units or bases differ.
Tests affine model stitching as a functional interchangeability measure, but not stitching layers, relative representations, or alignment without paired data.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are measured.

Tests dependence on stitching objective, invariance-aware versus standard data, and availability of predictive cues in image-classification settings. Does not test neighbour-count settings or broad out-of-distribution generalization.

Reports incomplete or differing functional alignment across model and training conditions, but does not establish that shared data or objectives, rather than a common model of reality, cause alignment.

rows.subject: ResNet-18 end model trained on CIFAR-10, with front models described as identity, cross-seed, cross-supervised, and cross-bias
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; cross-supervised front uses SimCLR followed by supervised classifier tuning
rows.operation_detail: Compared standard stitching agreement probability across stitching depth for front models with different information sources.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10 train and test splits; pixel-injected splits for cross-bias

rows.measure: Agreement probability with the standalone end model's predictions across stitching depth
rows.baseline: End-model agreement is 100% at the start of the stitching plot; standalone front-model agreement is Q at the end.
rows.value: The paper states that all formulations achieve high functional similarity in deep layers, including cross-bias.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged across three random initializations; no error bars or other uncertainty values stated.
rows.note: The text reports a shared qualitative result across formulations, not separate numerical values for each objective. The authors treat this high compatibility as potentially misleading because the front model uses different cues.
rows.check: Standard stitching gives high deep-layer agreement for all front models, including cross-bias, so it bears on V4 as observed. Alone it shows no metric dependence, so the V6 link is dropped; the V6 contrast lives in r2.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3 experimental setting and stitching-plot definition; Section 3.1, Figure 2 discussion.

rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch; cross-supervised front uses SimCLR followed by supervised classifier tuning
rows.operation_detail: Compared invariance-aware stitching agreement probability across stitching depth using inputs constructed to be identically represented by the front model at the stitch level.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10 train and test splits; pixel-injected splits for cross-bias
invariance-enabling formulations: SLM, DM, and FuLA

rows.measure: Agreement probability with the standalone end model's predictions across stitching depth
rows.baseline: Standard model stitching is the comparison condition; random chance is the stated reference for nonexistent functional similarity.
rows.value: The paper states that cross-bias similarity quickly diminishes to random chance and that similarity decreases more sharply as front-model semantic divergence increases.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged across three random initializations; no error bars or other uncertainty values stated.
rows.note: The paper reports qualitative trajectories, not numerical values. HLM is excluded because it is not invariance-enabling.
rows.check: State refers to V6: the same pairs judged compatible under standard stitching fall to chance (cross-bias) under invariance-aware stitching. For V4 the effect is partial: interchangeability degrades with front-model divergence. The V7 link is removed; the row says nothing about shared data or objectives as a cause.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, Figure 2 discussion: cross-bias agreement reaches chance under invariance-aware settings excluding HLM.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 end model stitched with a cross-task front model trained on LS-ImageNet-10
rows.operation_detail: Measured excessive agreement probability to assess use of pixel shortcuts during standard stitching.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10 variants: fixed-location class-specific pixel patterns, pixel-injected data, and pixel patterns replaced with random noise

rows.measure: Excessive agreement probability: agreement on pixel-injected test data minus agreement when pixel patterns are permuted across classes
rows.baseline: Agreement on the version with pixel patterns permuted across classes
rows.value: The text states that every formulation is susceptible to shortcut learning, with the effect diminishing as cues become less available across the three variants.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged across three randomly initialized runs; no error bars or other uncertainty values stated.
rows.note: The authors describe the outcomes qualitatively; no numerical excessive-agreement values are stated.
rows.check: Measures the stitching layer exploiting unseen pixel cues in a cross-task pair. This is an inflation of the similarity measure (V6), not interchangeability of learned representations. V4 and V7 links removed.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 end model stitched with a cross-task front model trained on LS-ImageNet-10
rows.operation_detail: Measured excessive agreement probability during invariance-aware stitching.

conditions.value: CIFAR-10 variants: fixed-location class-specific pixel patterns, pixel-injected data, and pixel patterns replaced with random noise
invariance-enabling formulations: SLM, DM, and FuLA

rows.measure: Excessive agreement probability: agreement on pixel-injected test data minus agreement when pixel patterns are permuted across classes
rows.baseline: Standard model stitching is the comparison condition; the noise-replaced variant is described as providing no shortcut cues.
rows.value: The text states that excessive agreement is greatly reduced, often approaching zero, and closely matches the noise-replaced condition.
rows.uncertainty: Results averaged across three randomly initialized runs; no error bars or other uncertainty values stated.
rows.note: The reported reduction is qualitative; the text does not say shortcut exploitation is eliminated in every case.
rows.check: Excessive agreement drops, often near zero, under invariance-aware stitching; the measured similarity depends on the procedure. V4 and V7 links removed.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 end model stitched with a cross-task front model trained on LS-ImageNet-10
rows.operation_detail: Compared shortcut use under invariance-aware SLM stitching with standard stitching and other invariance-enabling objectives.
rows.baseline: Standard model stitching and the invariance-aware DM and FuLA results are comparison conditions.
rows.value: Across additional architectures, the text states that invariance-aware SLM still engages in shortcut learning, but to a significantly lesser extent than standard stitching.
rows.note: The result is stated for the additional-architecture experiments; no numerical value is given.
rows.check: Shortcut use depends on the objective (SLM is still affected). The subject should note that it covers the additional architectures in Appendix F.3. V4 and V7 links removed.

rows.subject: CIFAR-10 cross-seed model pair
rows.stage_stated: trained from scratch with different random initializations
rows.operation_detail: Compared excessive agreement under standard and invariance-aware stitching for same-task, cross-seed models.

conditions.value: cross-seed, trained on the same task

rows.baseline: Standard stitching; the text says the effect is less pronounced in this cross-seed case to begin with.
rows.value: The text states that invariance-aware stitching mitigates unseen-cue exploitation in cross-seed stitching as well.
rows.check: Cross-seed shortcut inflation is smaller to begin with but is still reduced by invariance-aware stitching. V4 link removed.

rows.measure: Agreement probability with the standalone end model's predictions across stitching depth
